newsitem.title: FRANCE: French favour renegotiating Maastricht treaty - poll.
newsitem.headline: French favour renegotiating Maastricht treaty - poll.

text.p: A majority of voters want France to renegotiate conditions for joining the single European currency, according to an opinion poll on Thursday, the first such survey since a left-wing victory in a parliamentary election.
The Ipsos survey, to be published in the weekly Le Point, said a 52 to 36 percent majority favoured renegotiating the Maastricht treaty conditions for qualifying for the euro from 1999.

The Socialists, who lead the new government, want European construction to be re-focused towards growth and jobs and have promised they will not impose extra austerity to qualify for the euro. France narrowly approved the Maastricht treaty in a 1992 referendum.

Forty-six percent of 834 people questioned said they wanted conservative President Jacques Chirac to lead the renegotiation, while 37 percent preferred Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin to take the leading role.
Under French constitutional practice, the president has the leading role in foreign policy.

While 55 percent believed power-sharing between Chirac and Jospin was a good thing, 58 percent believed the arrangement, known as "cohabitation". would not last the five-year term of the National Assembly elected last Sunday.

The poll said 43 percent of voters approved Jospin's choice of a "pink-green-red" cabinet mixing Socialists and Greens with Communists and other leftists, to 19 percent who were dissatisfied and a large 38 percent who had no opinion.
Fifty per cent to 32 percent were satisfied with the inclusion of Communists ministers, who took three cabinet seats.
Turning to Jospin's proposed reforms, most voters backed cutting VAT on essential goods, raising the minimum wage and creating jobs for young people to curb record 12.8 percent unemployment.
A majority favoured reviewing the announced closure of carmaker Renault's Belgian factory in Vilvoorde and closing down the fault-prone Super-Phenix nuclear fast-breeder reactor in eastern France.
But most opposed the Socialists' intentions to repeal hardline laws to curb illegal immigration and halt plans to privatise France-Telecom.

As war raged for the leadership of the defeated right, a wide majority of 67 percent believed ex-prime minister Alain Juppe should hand over the Gaullist RPR party to his socially-minded rival Philippe Seguin.

Forty-five to 33 percent wanted the RPR and the centrist UDF to merge into a single party, and 65 to 25 percent said it should refuse any rapprochement with the far-right National Front which won nearly 15 percent of the vote in the election.
